extracted.intended_audience: educational institutions that receive Federal financial assistance (K-12 and postsecondary), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and institutional counsel
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX lactation and pregnancy compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts regulatory requirements and implementation guidance in final 34 C.F.R. §106.40 concerning (1) a recipient's obligation to ensure student access to lactation spaces, (2) limits on requiring supporting medical documentation for pregnancy- or lactation-related modifications, and (3) comparable treatment of pregnancy-related conditions to other temporary medical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient must ensure student access to a lactation space (§106.40(b)(3)(v))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must ensure that a student can access a lactation space that 'may be used' for pumping or breastfeeding as needed; provision of lactation space must be prompt and effective to prevent sex discrimination and ensure equal access to the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a lactation space meets standards is case-by-case but generally means the space is functional, appropriate, and safe for the student's use. The recipient must ensure access (not merely availability). The Department clarifies that if a student is permitted to bring a child into the education program (e.g., onsite childcare or visitor policy), they may breastfeed in the lactation space. Nothing in the final regulations precludes expressing breast milk or breastfeeding outside the designated lactation space where State or local law allows it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility on lactation space size, features, and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.40(b)(3)(v) does not prescribe particular size, shape, or structural features for a lactation space; recipients are not required to construct new lactation spaces if an existing space otherwise meets the requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department declines to adopt additional specific requirements (e.g., chair, flat surface, electrical outlet, running water, refrigerator) to preserve recipient flexibility and to allow for review alongside other Federal lactation laws. Recipients may offer additional features voluntarily or as reasonable modifications. State or local laws that require particular features are not preempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility considerations for location, number, hours, and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have discretion over where lactation spaces are located, the number of lactation spaces, and how they handle administration (including evening and weekend access), but must ensure that lack of access would not frustrate a lactating student's ability to participate in the education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include whether inability to access a space would prevent participation in classes, extracurriculars, or school-related events (including evenings/weekends). Administrative solutions may include signage, scheduling systems, or multi-person spaces separated by partitions that shield view and prevent intrusion. The Department expects access to be prompt and effective rather than merely theoretically available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient responsibility vs. Title IX Coordinator role
rubrics_metrics.description: The recipient (institution) is ultimately responsible for ensuring that a student can access a lactation space; the Title IX Coordinator must coordinate actions under §106.40(b)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised §106.40(b)(3) to clarify that it is the recipient's responsibility to take actions and the Title IX Coordinator's responsibility to coordinate specific actions under paragraphs (b)(3)(i) through (vi), including a student's access to a lactation space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on requiring supporting documentation except when necessary and reasonable (§106.40(b)(3)(vi))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must not require supporting documentation for requests under §106.40(b)(3)(ii) through (v) (reasonable modifications or specific actions for pregnancy or related conditions), unless the documentation is necessary and reasonable under the circumstances to determine the modifications to offer or other specific actions to take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department added §106.40(b)(3)(vi) to limit documentation requests. In virtually all situations, proceeding without documentation or relying on the student's self-attestation is least burdensome and fastest. Documentation should be requested only when needed to determine the appropriate modification (e.g., medically-ordered bed rest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary-and-reasonable standard for documentation requests
rubrics_metrics.description: When documentation is requested, it must be 'only that which is necessary and reasonable under the circumstances' and generally no more than sufficient to confirm—in a manner fair to the student—that the student has a need related to pregnancy or related conditions requiring a reasonable modification or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: requiring documentation to support medically-ordered bed rest may be necessary and reasonable; however, it would not be necessary and reasonable to request unrelated medical details (e.g., date of last menstrual cycle) or to re-confirm a pregnancy when the student already self-confirmed. A recipient may not deny a requested modification based on lack of documentation if the recipient's documentation request does not comport with §106.40(b)(3)(vi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-exhaustive list of situations where documentation is not necessary or reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.40(b)(3)(vi) provides examples when it is not necessary and reasonable to require documentation, and therefore a recipient may not require documentation in these circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed situations include: (1) when the student's need is obvious (e.g., self-confirmed pregnancy or physically obvious condition); (2) when the student has previously provided sufficient supporting documentation; (3) when the requested reasonable modification is one of four commonly sought adjustments (carrying/keeping water nearby and drinking; using a bigger desk; sitting or standing; taking breaks to eat, drink, or use the restroom); (4) when the need is lactation/pumping (medical documentation for initiation of lactation is uncommon and unnecessary); and (5) when the specific action is already available to students for non-pregnancy reasons without documentation (e.g., policies that permit limited absences without documentation). These situations are non-exhaustive and may overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment comparable to other temporary medical conditions (§106.40(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent consistent with paragraph (b)(3), a recipient must treat pregnancy or related conditions 'in the same manner and under the same policies as any other temporary medical condition' with respect to medical or hospital benefits, services, plans, or policies the recipient administers, operates, offers, or participates in for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department replaced proposed language referencing 'temporary disability' and 'physical condition' with 'temporary medical condition' to avoid implying pregnancy itself is a disability and to include psychological or emotional conditions as appropriate comparators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection with disability law — pregnancy is not a disability; disability protections still apply when present
rubrics_metrics.description: Pregnancy itself is not a disability under Section 504 or the ADA, but conditions or complications related to pregnancy may qualify as disabilities; where they do, those protections apply in addition to Title IX obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that §106.40(b)(4) applies regardless of whether pregnancy-related conditions qualify as disabilities. Recipients may sometimes need distinct processes or results under Title IX versus disability laws; this difference is acknowledged and should be managed to avoid confusion.
